title: OneDrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs & Changes
summary: OneDrive pricing options include a free plan and paid subscriptions with varying storage limits and features. Compare to find the right tier for you.
body_markdown:
## Automating OneDrive File Chores with Activepieces


Filing attachments, copying files to a second service and alerting you when a folder changes are all things Activepieces can do.


> Only if Microsoft 365 is paid for and used is OneDrive the cheapest of the four.


It is an open-source automation tool whose public repository holds 747 integrations, OneDrive among them, and whose core carries an MIT licence (the enterprise directories sit under a separate commercial one), so you're unlikely to hit integration limitations.


It doesn't do anything to what OneDrive costs or how much it holds, leaving OneDrive's pricing and storage limits in place.


Describe a chore such as filing email attachments into a named OneDrive folder in its built-in chat, and what comes back is a published flow, live in your account, with a run trace for every execution that lists each step and what it did.


That matters here because nothing in the earlier comparison moves: the bundled plan is still the cheapest, and the standalone plan still has no pricing edge.


### Tasks worth automating


In the screenshot below, a five-step workflow sits in the Activepieces builder: Webhook Trigger, Get from the database, Ask ChatGPT, Send SMS, then Put back to the database.


On the Free plan, which allows unlimited flows and 1,000 credits a month, a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, and AI steps like the ChatGPT one cost more, starting at 2 credits on a fast model.


The "Ask ChatGPT" step is selected, and its panel holds a Question field with instructions for a customer support agent and a Business Details block describing StoreX, an IT repair shop in San Francisco that fixes Apple devices and is open 8am to 10pm Pacific, every day.


It is a support-reply flow, not a OneDrive one, so take only the shape from it: a trigger, a few steps you can read in order, and a result at the end.


A OneDrive chore is built from the same blocks, so you can see what each step does before you switch it on.


Pick any of three chores and the shape holds. First, filing email attachments into a named OneDrive folder, so nobody drags them over by hand.


Second, copying new files to a second storage service, which gives you a backup that doesn't depend on a single vendor's account. Third, sending a message when something changes in a watched folder, so a shared drive stops being something you have to check.


### What automation doesn't fix about OneDrive storage costs


None of this changes your bill. Every file the automation saves still counts against your OneDrive storage, so a flow that files attachments all day fills the quota faster, and the per-terabyte math from earlier gets worse, not better.


A backup copy also lands in a second service you may pay for separately, which adds a cost line instead of removing one.


After purchase, the limits that bite, the 250 GB file size, the 400-character path and the 93-day recycle bin, stay exactly where Microsoft sets them. Activepieces works around OneDrive; none of its 747 integrations raises any of those ceilings.


Pick the plan on cost per terabyte and per user first, then decide whether the chores are worth automating.


Activepieces is the better fit for people who want to set up OneDrive file chores, such as filing email attachments into a named folder, by describing them in plain language rather than building them by hand or hiring someone to do it.


The built-in chat publishes a live flow in your account, and each run leaves a trace listing every step and what it did, so you can check the result yourself.


That advantage is about ease of setup and visibility, not cost: OneDrive's pricing and storage limits stay as they are, and the earlier comparison on price is unchanged.
